summary: This document specifies a DHCPv6 option for exchanging information about a client's fully qualified domain name and about who is responsible for updating the DNS resource records related to the client's address assignments.

plainLanguage.summary: DNS keeps two records for each host: one that maps its name to its address, and one that maps the address back to a name. This RFC lets a DHCPv6 client give its name to the server and say which of the two records it will update itself, so that both sides agree on who does what.

questions: what is the dhcpv6 client fqdn option
what do the s o and n flags mean in dhcpv6 fqdn
subtitle: How a DHCPv6 client tells the server its domain name, and who then updates the DNS records.

tldr.problem: When a site hands out an IPv6 address with DHCPv6, the DNS records that map the host's name to its address and back have to be kept in step, and nobody had defined how the client and the server should divide that job.
tldr.mechanism: A new DHCPv6 option, code 39, carries the client's fully qualified domain name and three flag bits. The S, O and N bits tell the server whether it should update the AAAA record, the PTR record, both or neither.
tldr.outcome: Client and server agree on who updates which DNS record, and the RFC suggests record lifetimes that match the lease. Name conflicts are left to a separate document.

facts.label: Suggested record lifetime ceiling
facts.value: One third of the lease lifetime

facts.label: Messages that may carry the option

today: RFC 4704 is a Proposed Standard from October 2006, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The option code 39 was assigned by IANA, and the related DHCPv4 option is in RFC 4702. Name conflict handling is left to RFC 4703.

sections.title: What the Client FQDN Option Is For
sections.content:
DNS maintains, among other things, the information about the mapping between hosts' fully qualified domain names and the IPv6 addresses assigned to the hosts. That information is held in two types of resource record: AAAA and PTR. The DNS update specification in RFC 2136 describes a mechanism that enables DNS information to be updated over a network.

The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 provides a mechanism by which a host, a DHCPv6 client, can acquire configuration information along with its stateful IPv6 addresses. This document specifies a new DHCPv6 option, the Client FQDN option, which DHCPv6 clients and servers use to exchange information about the client's fully qualified domain name and about who has the responsibility for updating the DNS with the associated AAAA and PTR records.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS holds a record that maps a host's name to its address and another that maps the address back. DHCPv6 hands out the address, so something has to keep those records in step. This RFC adds an option through which the client and the server say who will do it.

sections.title: Two Models of Operation
sections.content:
When a DHCPv6 client acquires an address, the site's administrator may want the AAAA record for the client's fully qualified domain name and the PTR record for the acquired address to be updated. Acquiring an address involves two entities, a client and a server, and in principle each could perform none, one or both of the DNS update transactions. In practice, the option is primarily intended to work in two cases: the client updates the AAAA record and the server updates the PTR record, or the server updates both. The only difference between the two cases is whether the FQDN-to-address mapping is updated by the client or by the server. The address-to-FQDN mapping is updated by the server in both cases.

These two cases matter because of authority over the DNS domain names. A client may be given authority over mapping its own AAAA records, or that authority may be restricted to a server to stop the client listing arbitrary addresses or associating its addresses with arbitrary domain names. In all cases, the only reasonable place for the authority over the PTR records associated with the address is in the server that allocates the address.

A third case is supported, in which the client asks the server to perform no updates, but it is presumed to be rare because of the authority issues. Whether a site permits all, some or no DHCPv6 servers and clients to perform DNS updates into the zones it controls is entirely a matter of local administrative policy. The range of policies is very broad, from sites where only the servers hold credentials the DNS servers accept, to sites where each individual client has been configured with credentials that let it modify its own domain name. The specification applies only to DHCPv6 client and server processes; it does not apply to other processes that initiate DNS updates.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two sensible arrangements. Either the client keeps its own name record up to date and the server keeps the reverse record, or the server does both. The split matters for authority: a client that can edit its own name record could also claim other names, so some sites keep all the editing at the server.

sections.title: The Option and Its Flags
sections.content:
To update the address-to-FQDN mapping, a DHCPv6 server needs to know the FQDN of the client for the addresses in the client's IA_NA bindings. To let the client convey its FQDN, this document defines a new DHCPv6 option called Client FQDN. The code for this option is 39 and its minimum length is 1 octet. The option holds the option code, the option length, a flags field and the domain name, whose length is the option length minus one. The Client FQDN option must only appear in a message's options field, and it applies to all addresses for all IA_NA bindings in the transaction.

The flags field is one octet holding four flag bits and the rest reserved. The S bit indicates whether the server should or should not perform the AAAA record, the FQDN-to-address, DNS updates. A client sets the bit to 0 to say the server should not perform the updates and to 1 to say it should. The state of the bit in the server's reply indicates the action taken by the server; if it is 1, the server has taken responsibility for AAAA record updates for the FQDN.

The O bit indicates whether the server has overridden the client's preference for the S bit. A client must set this bit to 0, and a server must set it to 1 if the S bit in its reply does not match the S bit it received.

The N bit indicates whether the server should not perform any DNS updates. A client sets it to 0 to request that the server should perform updates, the PTR record and possibly the AAAA record based on the S bit, or to 1 to request that the server should not perform any DNS updates. A server sets the N bit to say whether the server shall, at 0, or shall not, at 1, perform DNS updates. If the N bit is 1, the S bit must be 0.

The remaining bits are reserved for future assignment. Clients and servers that send the option must clear the reserved bits and must ignore them when reading.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is number 39 and holds the client's name plus three flags. The S flag asks the server to look after the name record. The N flag asks the server to do no DNS work at all. The O flag is the server saying that it has ignored the client's preference. Any spare bits are set to zero and ignored.

sections.title: The Domain Name Field
sections.content:
The domain name part of the option carries all or part of the fully qualified domain name of a DHCPv6 client. The data must be encoded as described in section 8 of RFC 3315. In order to determine whether the FQDN has changed between message exchanges, the client and server must not alter the domain name field contents unless the FQDN has actually changed.

A client may be configured with a fully qualified domain name, or with a partial name that is not fully qualified. If a client knows only part of its name, it may send a name that is not fully qualified, indicating that it knows part of the name but does not necessarily know the zone in which the name is to be embedded. To send a fully qualified domain name, the domain name field is set to the DNS-encoded name including the terminating zero-length label. To send a partial name, it is set to the DNS-encoded name without the terminating zero-length label. A client may also leave the domain name field empty if it wants the server to provide a name. Servers should send the complete fully qualified domain name in Client FQDN options.
sections.plainLanguage: The name travels in the DNS wire format. A client that knows only part of its name can send that part, leaving off the final empty label, and a client with no name at all can send an empty field and let the server choose one.

sections.title: What the Client Does
sections.content:
A client must only include the Client FQDN option in SOLICIT, REQUEST, RENEW or REBIND messages. A client that sends the option must also include the option in the Option Request option if it expects the server to include the Client FQDN option in any responses.

A client that owns and maintains its own fully qualified domain name, and wants to be responsible for updating the FQDN-to-address mapping, must include the option in its SOLICIT with Rapid Commit, REQUEST, RENEW and REBIND messages, and may include it in its other SOLICIT messages. The S, O and N bits must all be 0. Once the client's configuration is complete, meaning it has received a REPLY and successfully completed a final check on the parameters in it, the client may start an update for its AAAA records, unless the server set the S bit to 1. If the S bit is 1, the client should not update the name in the server's returned domain name field. A client explicitly configured with a fully qualified domain name may ignore the state of the S bit if the server's returned name matches the client's configured name.

A client that wants the server to do the updates sets the S bit to 1 and the O and N bits to 0. A client that wants no server-side DNS updates sets the N bit to 1 and the S and O bits to 0. In that last case, once its configuration is complete the client may do its own DNS updates as long as the server's N bit is 1. If the server's N bit is 0, the server may perform the PTR record updates, and may also perform the AAAA record updates if the S bit is 1.

A client that delegates the FQDN-to-address mapping to a server gets no indication, positive or negative, of whether the server managed the update. The client may use a DNS query to check whether the mapping is up to date, but because of load on the servers and DNS propagation delays it can only infer success. If a client releases an address before the valid lifetime expires and the client is responsible for updating its AAAA record, it should delete that record before sending the RELEASE message. A client that has not been able to delete an AAAA record it added should try to notify its administrator. A client should not perform DNS updates to AAAA records for its non-global unicast addresses or its temporary addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The client says in the option whether it will do the name update itself or wants the server to do it. After the lease is confirmed, the client may then update the DNS, unless the server took that job on. The server never reports back whether the update worked, so a client that wants to check has to query DNS and can only guess from the answer.

sections.title: What the Server Does
sections.content:
Servers must only include a Client FQDN option in ADVERTISE and REPLY messages if the client included the option and the option is requested in the Option Request option of the client's message.

The server examines its configuration and the flag bits in the client's option to decide how to respond. It sets the S, O and N bits to 0 in the copy of the option it returns. If the client's N bit is 1 and the server's configuration allows it to honour the request for no server-initiated DNS updates, the server sets the N bit to 1. Otherwise, if the client's S bit is 1 and the server's configuration allows it to honour the request for the server to do the AAAA updates, the server sets the S bit to 1, and if that does not match the client's S bit it also sets the O bit to 1.

The server may be configured to use the name supplied in the client's option, or to modify the supplied name or substitute a different one. It should send its notion of the complete fully qualified domain name for the client in the domain name field, and may simply copy the field from the client's option.

The server should not perform any DNS updates if the N bit is 1 in the option of the REPLY it is about to send, but it should delete any records it previously added for the client. It may perform the PTR record update unless the N bit is 1, and it may perform the AAAA record update if the S bit is 1 in the option of the REPLY it is about to send. It may perform these updates even if the client's message did not carry the option, and it must not initiate DNS updates when responding with an ADVERTISE message. It may complete its updates before or after sending the REPLY. If the AAAA update finishes only after the reply, the server's later interaction with the DNS server may cause it to change the domain name it associates with the client, for example if it detects and resolves a domain-name conflict, in which case the name it returns to the client would change between two exchanges. If the server previously performed updates for the client and the client's information has not changed, it may skip further updates.

When a server receives a RELEASE or DECLINE for an address, detects that the valid lifetime has expired, or ends a binding early by sending a REPLY with a zero valid lifetime, it should delete any PTR record it associated with the address. If the server took responsibility for AAAA records, it should delete those as well.
sections.plainLanguage: The server returns the option only if the client asked for it, and sets the flags to match what its own policy allows. It can keep the client's name, change it or replace it, and should send back the full name it settled on. When the lease ends, the server removes the DNS records it added.

sections.title: Choosing DNS Record Lifetimes
sections.content:
Records associated with DHCP clients may be more volatile than statically configured records. DHCP clients and servers that perform dynamic updates should try to specify resource record lifetimes that reflect this volatility, in order to minimise the possibility that answers to DNS queries return records that refer to address assignments that have expired or been released.

The coupling among primary, secondary and caching DNS servers is loose, and it is impossible to prevent all situations in which a resolver may return a record reflecting an expired or released address. In deployment this rarely represents a significant problem. Most DHCP-managed clients are infrequently looked up by name in the DNS, and the deployment of incremental zone transfer and NOTIFY can reduce the latency between updates and their visibility at secondary servers.

The RFC suggests basic guidelines for implementers. In general, the lifetimes for records added as a result of address assignment should be less than the initial lifetime. The record lifetime on a DNS record added should not exceed one third of the lifetime, but should not be less than 10 minutes. Individual administrators will have varying requirements, so DHCP servers and clients should allow administrators to configure the lifetime and its upper and lower bounds, either as an absolute time interval or as a percentage of the lease lifetime. While clients and servers may update the lifetime of the records as the lease is about to expire, there is no requirement that they do so, as this puts additional load on the DNS system with likely little benefit.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS records for DHCP clients go stale quickly, so they should carry short lifetimes. The RFC suggests a lifetime of no more than a third of the lease and no less than ten minutes, and asks implementations to let the administrator set those bounds.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Name Conflicts
sections.content:
Unauthenticated updates to the DNS can lead to tremendous confusion, through malicious attack or through inadvertent misconfiguration. Administrators need to be wary of permitting unsecured DNS updates to zones that are exposed to the global Internet. Both DHCPv6 clients and servers should use some form of update request origin authentication, such as secure DNS dynamic update, when performing DNS updates.

Whether a client is responsible for updating its name mapping or whether that is the responsibility of the server is a site-local matter, likely based on the security model used with the DNS update protocol, for example where only the client holds sufficient credentials. Whether the server is always responsible for the mapping, regardless of the wishes of an individual client, is also a site-local matter. In cases where a server is performing DNS updates on behalf of a client, it should be sure of the DNS name to use for the client and of the identity of the client. Depending on the presence of or type of authentication used with the DHCPv6 Authentication option, a server may not have much confidence in the identities of its clients.

This document does not resolve how a client or server prevents name conflicts; it addresses only how they negotiate the fully qualified domain name and who performs the DNS updates. Implementers will need to consider how name conflicts will be prevented. If a DNS updater needs a security token to perform updates on a specific name, conflicts can only occur if multiple updaters are given a token for that name. Or, if the fully qualified domains are based on the specific address bound to a client, conflicts will not occur. Or, a name conflict resolution technique should be used. It is critical to implement proper conflict resolution, and the security considerations of conflict resolution apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone allowed to update the DNS without authenticating can cause a great deal of confusion, so both sides should authenticate their updates. This RFC does not say what happens when two machines claim the same name; that is left to a separate document on resolving name conflicts.

messages.note: Carries the client's domain name and the flag bits.

messages.note: Adds or removes the AAAA and PTR records.

viz.caption: THE OPTION FIELDS AS PRINTED IN THE RFC

data.title: DHCPv6 Client FQDN option
data.code:
option-code      OPTION_CLIENT_FQDN (39)
option-len       1 + length of domain name
flags            flag bits used between client and server to
                 negotiate who performs which updates
domain-name      the partial or fully qualified domain name
                 (with length option-len - 1)

viz.caption: THE THREE FLAG BITS IN THE FLAGS FIELD

items.title: S
items.text: Set by the client to 1 to ask the server to do the AAAA record update, the one that maps the name to the address.

items.title: O
items.text: Set by the server to 1 when the S bit in its reply does not match the S bit the client sent.

items.title: N
items.text: Set to 1 to ask for no server DNS updates at all. When it is 1, the S bit must be 0.
